in patients with perisellar tumour, a blockade of the cerebro-ocular circulation of the cere- brospinal fluid may lead to a glaucomatous cupping of the disc, which is definitely not a specific feature of glaucoma.

in patients with compression of the optic nerves and chiasma by large perisellar masses, the level of BDNTr in the cerebrosporal fluid (CSF) is definitely reduced, whereas the CSF pressure is definitely raised.
the level of BDNFBDNF is definitely reduced in the optic nerve and retina in patients with glaucoma and that this reduction is definitely specific for glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

two main pathomechanisms of glaucoma: a direct blockade of the axoplasmic retrograde flow in the optic nerve and an additional blockade of the circulation from the intracral subarachnoid space into the orbital subarachnoidal space.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the blockade of the retrograd axoplasmic transport by the tumour is a pathomechanical event that is common for all optic nerve compressive lesions.

the pathomechanism of the glaucoma-like optic nerve damage in patients with large intracranial space-occupying tumours is a combination of the direct mechanical compression of the intraneural axons and the blockade of the circulation from the intracerebral to the orbital cerebrospinal CSF space.

in glaucoma, a blockade of the retrobulbar circulation of the cere-brospinal fluid is present, which leads to a reduction of the retrolaminar cere-bral spinal fluid pressure and a reduction in the retrograde axonal flow of BDNF, which is a growth factor for the retinal ganglionic cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optic nerve compression in perisellar tumour leads to a glaucomatous cupping of the disc, which is usually not seen in any other optic neuropathies.

the blockade of the circulation in the optic nerve canal by the large tumours may lead to an increase of the intracerebrospinal fluid-pressure in the subarachnoidal space surrounding the optic nerves and the chiasm, leading to an increase of pressure within the optic nerves.

the glaucoma-like optic neuropathy in large perisellar optic nerve tumours is not only caused by direct compression of the optic nerve but also by a blockade of CSF flow in the subarachnoid spaces of the orbit.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a large perisellar mass, in particular a large craniopharyngioma or a large pituitary adenoma, may lead to an increase in intracranial pressure and a reduction in cerebrospinal CSF pressure in the orbit.
a blockade of cerebrospinal CSF circulation may be an important factor in the development of glaucoma in patients with large tumours in perisellar location.
a glaucoma in perisellar tumour patients may be caused by a combination of direct compression of the optic nerves and chiasma and by the blockade of cerebrospinal circulation.
